You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_id = "1;2;3", text = "Although the final sample size (n = 46 and n = 50) provided 80% power to detect moderateto-large between-group differences (Cohen's d ≥ 0.58; two-sided α = 0.05), it was underpowered for the observed difference in cold occurrence (estimated power ≈ 40%)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p > 0.20", Text = "Among participants who developed colds (infection-only analysis), no statistically significant differences were observed between the probiotic and placebo groups in terms of the number of discomfort days, average discomfort score, peak discomfort score, or AUC (all p > 0.20; Table 2)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. live_data_statements: Recruitment of participants and study subjects Middle-aged and older adults aged between 50 and 75 years were recruited.
Prior to enrollment, all potential participants were required to complete a comprehensive health screening questionnaire to evaluate their medical history.

A total of 102 eligible participants provided informed consent and were enrolled in this randomized, double-blind, placebocontrolled trial. preprint (which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted medRxiv a license to display the preprint in periods, participants were instructed to maintain their usual daily routines and dietary habits to minimize potential confounding from lifestyle and dietary changes.

Throughout the 12-week trial, the participants were required to maintain daily and weekly health records, including completion of the Wisconsin Upper Respiratory Symptom Survey (WURSS-24), to monitor the incidence and severity of respiratory symptoms, as well as weekly documentation of vaccination status and common cold-related events.
During the study period, the participants completed daily questionnaires assessing upper respiratory symptoms.
A total of 102 volunteers were initially recruited for this study (Figure 1) and randomly assigned to the placebo group (n = 51) or the probiotic group (n = 51).

During the intervention, six participants were excluded: one in the placebo group (due to illness) and five in the probiotic group (one due to illness, two due to refusal to undergo a second blood test, and two due to missing questionnaire data).
First, the participants were generally healthy individuals with relatively mild baseline symptoms, limiting the potential for measurable improvement.
Informed consent was obtained from all subjects involved in the study.
Before the experiment, the researchers explained the experimental process in detail, and the experiment began after the subjects signed the consent form.
The participants were randomly assigned to either the probiotic group (n = 51) or the placebo group (n = 51) for a 12-week intervention period.
